p: Which two statements about the Cisco-IOS-XE-native model are true? (Choose two.)
o: It only holds operational state, so it can't be used to change configuration
Its structure follows the IOS XE CLI hierarchy
It covers platform features that the IETF and OpenConfig models don't
It's vendor-neutral, so the same payload works on other vendors' devices
It's maintained by the IETF NETMOD working group as a standard
e: Native models mirror the CLI and give the widest coverage of IOS XE features. They're Cisco-specific, and they hold configuration, while state lives mostly in the -oper models.

p: A script must read CPU utilization from an IOS XE switch. Which kind of model holds it?
o: A Cisco-IOS-XE-*-oper model, such as Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper, which holds read-only state
ietf-interfaces, under each interface's statistics
An OpenConfig config container, which reports the applied value of each setting alongside the intended one
Cisco-IOS-XE-native, under the process configuration
e: The -oper models are config false, built for operational data such as CPU, memory and interface counters. Native is for configuration.

p: How can a client find out which OpenConfig nodes a particular IOS XE release doesn't implement?
o: Read the OpenConfig model's description statements, which list the vendors and releases that don't support each node
Send edit-config requests for every node and record which ones fail
Read the deviation modules the device advertises, which mark nodes not-supported or changed
Compare the OpenConfig model with Cisco-IOS-XE-native line by line
e: Deviations, such as cisco-xe-openconfig-interfaces-deviation, formally describe where an implementation differs from the published model, so clients can adapt without trial and error.

p: In openconfig-interfaces, where does a client set an interface's MTU, and where does it read the value actually in effect?
o: Set .../interface/state/mtu, and read .../interface/config/mtu
Set and read both at .../interface/mtu, because OpenConfig has a single node
Set .../interface/config/mtu, and read it back from the same node
Set .../interface/config/mtu, and read .../interface/state/mtu
e: OpenConfig separates intended values (config, read-write) from applied and operational values (state, read-only). Comparing them shows whether a change has taken effect.

o: From the running datastore with get-config, which includes state
Under /interfaces/interface, where ro nodes now sit beside the configuration (NMDA)
Under /interfaces-state/interface, because NMDA keeps state in a separate tree from configuration
Under an -oper model only, because ietf-interfaces holds no state

Both, because each model keeps its own separate copy of the configuration on the device
